title: A Question Worth Asking
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 24 of 40
content:
I asked Iroh who he was when nobody wanted anything from him.

The question came out while we were carrying the last dry towels to the balcony above the Jasmine Dragon. Below us, Ba Sing Se filled with evening carts and the smell of cooking oil. Someone had started singing three streets away, loudly and not particularly well.

Iroh looked up at the sky. "A man who likes a quiet balcony."

"That's a place, not a person."

"A man who has brought you to a very good place."

"You're doing it again."

He took the towels from me and made a show of folding them. "What am I doing?"

"Answering the question that makes you sound most helpful."

He stopped folding.

I wished, for one terrible moment, that I'd simply asked whether he wanted more tea. It would have been easier. But I wasn't falling in love with an answer to every problem. I was falling for someone who could make a joke, and make another joke, and still carry something so heavy I sometimes saw it in the way he stood up.

Iroh sat on the little bench. There was room beside him, but he didn't pat it. He waited.

"I used to be many things," he said. "Some of them I did not choose. Others I chose badly."

"I know."

"I am also a man who sings off-key when he thinks no one can hear."

"That one's new."

"It is a carefully guarded secret."

From the street, the unknown singer missed another note so spectacularly Iroh winced. Then he began humming the same tune and made it worse on purpose. I laughed hard enough to lean against the railing.

"You're terrible."

"Then I have answered at least one part of your question."

We sat for a while. The breeze lifted the edge of his sleeve. I noticed a tiny scorch mark from the kettle he had nearly dropped that afternoon while arguing with a supplier over the cost of dried jasmine. I touched the fabric.

"Does this happen often?"

"Only when I am attempting to look dignified."

"So daily."

"An outrageous accusation."

I pulled my chair closer. "I mean it. What would you do if nobody was waiting for advice, nobody called you General or Uncle, and you could choose the afternoon for yourself?"

He thought longer than I expected.

"I would eat something sweet that I had no intention of sharing," he admitted. "I would play Pai Sho badly, so no one invited me to a serious match. I would visit a garden where nobody knew my name."

"Could you do any of that tomorrow?"

"Perhaps not the garden. Mina needs me to sign the delivery order, and Lian is waiting for us to repair the hose."

"That's two things. Not an entire lifetime."

He smiled, but I could see the uncertainty beneath it.

"I've spent so much of my life being useful in order to justify the room I occupied," he said. "I find it difficult to imagine occupying a room for pleasure."

I reached for his hand, then stopped. "Would you like me to hold it?"

"Yes."

His palm was warm. It still surprised me when something that simple felt like a choice two people had made together rather than an answer one person owed.

"I'm not asking you to stop helping people," I said. "But you can want things that have nothing to do with rescuing me."

"And what do you want?"

"I want you to stop making me guess whether there's a person behind the wise expression."

"Very demanding."

"Extremely."

He turned toward me. "Then I will tell you something selfish. When you leave to spend time with people you also love, I sometimes look at the upper room and wish you were in it. It is not a wish I intend to use against you."

I swallowed. We'd spoken plainly about my ethical non-monogamy and my preference for polyamory. Iroh had not been asked to pretend that he never missed me. I just didn't want longing to become a debt.

"You can say you miss me," I told him. "You can ask whether I'm free next week. I want to hear what you need, not discover it after you've become lonely enough to be noble about it."

His laugh was smaller this time. "Noble loneliness is a remarkably foolish habit."

"One you've perfected."

"I am reconsidering my achievements."

The shop bell rang downstairs. Mina called that the parcel runner had delivered the repaired tea strainer and wanted a receipt. Iroh rose, then glanced at me.

"Would you mind if I took care of that?"

"Not at all. I'll still be here."

He went down and came back five minutes later with a paper bag.

"Sweet buns," he announced. "Bought with my own money, so the inventory will not suffer."

"You bought two."

"I have not yet learned selfishness perfectly."

We ate them on the bench. He got sugar on his beard. I considered telling him, then decided I liked the excuse to lean closer. I wiped it away with my thumb. He caught my wrist gently.

"May I kiss you?" he asked.

"Please."

We kissed until the evening voices rose and the last light slipped between the rooftops. When we broke apart, he rested his head against my shoulder for a while.

"Call me Iroh when we're alone," he said.

"I already do."

"Then keep doing it. I like the way you say it."

Below, the city went on needing things. Above it, the man beside me wanted another sweet bun and someone to laugh with. That was more than enough for tonight.
